case20v1-req.as.prompt:
Rehri Technologies: The Spec the Builder Read

A teaching case on the spec as a prompt for an AI builder

1. Opening

On the morning of Monday 19 October 2026, Chaitrika Jassal, head of product at Rehri Technologies, stood at a whiteboard in the company's Baner office in Pune. The list in front of her had not existed the previous Tuesday. It had eleven lines. Each marked a place where an AI app builder, handed the fourteen-page product requirements document (PRD) for Rehri's new retailer credit feature, had been forced to choose between two readings of her own sentences, and had quietly chosen one.

She had until Friday 23 October to decide how the feature would be built. Sprint planning was at ten on Monday 26 October. Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November, the busiest fortnight of the year for her customers. Three paths were open, and she would have to defend whichever she took that Friday evening to colleagues and a client across five time zones.

2. Company background

Rehri was founded in Pune in 2019 by two engineers who had previously worked for a packaged-goods distributor. It sells ordering and invoicing software to distributors, the stockists who supply biscuits, soap and tea to neighbourhood kirana shops, and to the retailers who order from them. By March 2026 it served 640 distributors and 2.9 lakh retailers, had carried ₹4,200 crore of orders through the platform during the year, and had booked revenue of ₹86 crore. It employed 310 people, including 22 engineers in Bengaluru and Pune.

The market around it is crowded. Udaan and Jumbotail sell to kiranas directly as marketplaces, while Rehri works inside the distributor's own business and leaves the relationship with the retailer where it was. Khatabook and OkCredit keep digital ledgers for small shops. Retailers pay distributors mostly through UPI, and every order produces a GST invoice. Rehri's distributors carry brands such as Parle, Amul and Tata Consumer Products.

3. The situation

Credit was the part of the business Rehri's software only recorded. A kirana owner in Nashik who wanted a month's stock of tea and detergent on credit telephoned the distributor's salesman, who consulted a notebook. Exhibit 3 shows how much rode on that notebook: in the four weeks before Diwali 2025, credit orders were ₹133 crore of ₹410 crore, or 32.4 per cent, and the share rose every week. Chaitrika's feature, Udhaar Limit, would give each retailer a limit, show the balance at checkout and stop an order that crossed it. Rehri would not lend. The distributor would extend credit and Rehri would record it, a line counsel had advised holding in view of the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending rules.

PRD v3 had been signed off on 2 October by operations, finance, engineering and design. On Tuesday 13 October Chaitrika pasted it whole into an AI app builder. Forty minutes later she had a clickable retailer app and a distributor dashboard. Over the next three days her team listed eleven points where the builder had settled between two readings. Six were cosmetic. Five changed what a retailer could buy, and Rehri's finance team priced them at up to ₹180 lakh of credit wrongly extended or blocked across four weeks of last year's orders at 40 distributors (Exhibit 1; rows overlap, so the sum is a ceiling).

The team read the result from where each sat. The designer in Berlin, whose comments reached Pune each evening, found that the builder showed blocked retailers a bare "Limit exceeded" on a screen the PRD never mentioned. The data scientist in Toronto reran last year's orders under two readings of "overdue" and produced two different lists of blocked retailers. In Singapore, Charmila Jawanda telephoned six distributors and heard "monthly" used both ways. In New Jersey, Chitwan Johal had promised a large Dubai trading group, whose Indian companies accounted for 22 of Rehri's distributors, a demonstration of credit limits on Friday 30 October. Figure 1 places these dates in order, and Exhibit 2 sets out the three routes.

4. The people

Chaitrika Jassal, head of product in Pune, wrote PRD v3 and has run product for six years. She wants Rehri's first credit release to be one that distributors trust.

Chanpreet Jandial, engineering manager in Bengaluru, leads the 22 engineers. His last two features ran two weeks over, and both had begun with questions the PRD did not answer. He wants a specification he can estimate and a team that is not rewriting generated code he did not choose.

Chitwan Johal, head of sales in New Jersey, owns the Dubai relationship and the promise of 30 October. He regards the prototype as most of the way to a product. He wants live distributors before Diwali, when attention to new tools is at its highest.

Charmila Jawanda, customer-success lead in Singapore, has spent four years on calls with distributors. She wants the rules to match how credit is actually extended in the trade.

5. Exhibits

6. The options

Option A: build PRD v3 as written. Planning goes ahead on 26 October with the document that four functions signed. Chanpreet puts the build at ten weeks, and it costs ₹48.0 lakh (Exhibit 2). The Dubai demonstration on 30 October would show only the existing ordering screens.

Option B: revise the PRD from the builder's output, then build. Chaitrika rewrites the PRD and regenerates the prototype, with Charmila, finance and a few distributors. Engineers start on 2 November for nine weeks, at ₹45.2 lakh. Go-live matches Option A. The Diwali window passes without a credit pilot.

Option C: harden the prototype for a Diwali pilot. Three engineers spend the week of 26 October adding GST invoicing and security to the generated code, and 40 distributors go live on 2 November for ₹2.4 lakh. Chitwan's demonstration would run on live software. The generated code would be kept or rebuilt after the pilot.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What did the builder's output show about PRD v3 that four functions had not found when they signed it?
  2. Using Exhibits 1 and 3, which of the five points would matter most to a distributor during the Diwali window, and what would you want to know before ranking them?
  3. What does each option assume about who resolves the eleven points, and when?
  4. If you were Chaitrika Jassal, which option would you present on Friday 23 October, and what would you say to Chanpreet and Chitwan?

8. A note for the learner

Treating a spec as a prompt turns the builder into a reader with no shared history. It cannot lean on what finance obviously meant, so each place it guesses is a place the document is open to more than one reading. That evidence arrives in forty minutes and costs a few credits, before a team of six has spent ten weeks.

A well-reasoned answer separates the points that carry money from those that can wait, prices the delay honestly, and keeps a promise to a client apart from a promise to put untested rules in front of paying distributors.

One defensible path is Option B with a boundary. Chaitrika closes the five money points in the week of 26 October, records each decision in PRD v4, and regenerates the prototype to confirm the builder now reads it as intended. Chitwan takes the revised prototype, on sample data, to Dubai on 30 October, so his commitment holds without live credit. The revision adds ₹2.0 lakh and one week of start, yet B totals ₹45.2 lakh against A's ₹48.0 lakh and reaches the same January go-live, and it moves five arguments from the sprint, where each costs engineering time, to the week before it, where each costs a conversation. Diwali is forgone knowingly, not by default.
case40v1-req.as.prompt:
Sirjan Health Technologies: Thirty-One Choices Nobody Made

A teaching case on handing a product requirements document to an AI builder

1. Mohali, Sunday 15 November 2026

The office in Sector 67 was empty except for the security desk and Dilpreet Kathuria, who had come in at eight because the flat was full of relatives. On the wall behind her were thirty-one index cards in two columns. She had sorted them on Saturday and no longer trusted the sort: thirteen cards where an AI app builder had read a sentence of her own product requirements document one way when she had meant it another, and eighteen where she could not reconstruct having meant anything at all.

At half past nine the next morning she would tell the steering committee what Sirjan Health Technologies should build, and when. Six of the thirty-one carried a number: ₹371.8 lakh a month of exposure, before removing double-counted claims, if the Shortfall Desk shipped as the prototype had rendered it (Exhibit 1). She had until then to decide whether the cards were a defect list, a specification, or an indictment of the way her team wrote.

2. The company, and the decision of 2021

Sirjan was founded in Mohali in 2018 by Darshil Kataria and two classmates from a Chandigarh engineering college to do one thing: carry a hospital's cashless pre-authorisation request to an insurer and bring the answer back. In the year to 31 March 2026 it booked revenue of ₹94 crore. It now serves 286 Indian hospitals, connects nine insurers and third-party administrators, and employs 268 people, 64 of them engineers split between Bengaluru and Pune.

The decision that shapes today was taken in 2021. Offered a configurable adjudication engine that would have taken a year, or hand-coding each insurer's rules in a small internal language the team called the rulebook, Kataria chose the rulebook. It won Sirjan its first six insurer connections in fourteen months and it is now 1,340 rules deep, maintained by two claims analysts in Mohali, with a median of nine working days to change one. In 2024, to close a hospital group burned by a silent change in a rival's logic, the master services agreement acquired a clause: no change in adjudication behaviour without twenty working days' written notice. It is now in every Indian contract Sirjan signs.

3. The industry

Indian health claims are in the middle of being rewired. The National Health Claims Exchange, built by the National Health Authority with the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India behind it, is replacing a decade of bilateral portals with one protocol; the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission supplies the identifiers; Bima Sugam is meant to do the same for distribution. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs what a hospital may tell a vendor about a patient, and on whose consent.

Sirjan's competition comes from three directions. Established administrators such as Medi Assist sit on the insurer side of the same pipe. Claims-automation firms, Vitraya among them, sell the adjudication itself. And the largest hospital groups — the scale at which Apollo Hospitals and Max Healthcare operate — increasingly build the module inside their own information systems. Sirjan's exposure outside India is one large contract: Qasr Medical Group's nine hospitals in Dubai, ₹7.2 crore a year, 7.7 per cent of revenue, running on a separate single-tenant deployment that must remain resident in the United Arab Emirates. Figure 1 sets out who exchanges what with whom.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The Shortfall Desk was Kathuria's answer to a complaint that filled Sirjan's support queue. When an insurer raises a shortfall query on a pre-authorisation — a demand for a discharge summary, an investigation report, a clarification of the line of treatment — the hospital's billing team must answer it while the clock on the admission runs. In September 2026 the platform carried 1,02,000 pre-authorisation requests and 34,000 of them, 33.3 per cent, drew at least one query (Exhibit 4). The Desk was to put every open query in one inbox, age it, and escalate it.

PRD v4, twenty-two pages, was signed off on Friday 2 October by product, engineering, the rulebook team, design and finance. Everyone who signed it had read it. On Monday 2 November Kathuria pasted the whole document into an AI app builder and asked for a working front end against Sirjan's sandbox API. By Wednesday 4 November there was a clickable inbox, an ageing view, a query-response screen and an escalation queue, and the team demonstrated it to Kataria.

Four people then reviewed the prototype against the document, independently, on Thursday 5 and Friday 6 November. What came back was not a bug list. It was thirty-one places where the builder had resolved an ambiguity in the text, usually without comment (Exhibit 2). The Monday 9 November triage classed six as material and priced them (Exhibit 1). Three beliefs held on 2 October have since failed: that the document was unambiguous because five functions had signed it; that the ambiguities, once found, would be few and cosmetic; and that the rulebook could absorb whatever the prototype settled, which the notice clause makes false for anything changing what a hospital is told it will be paid. On Tuesday 10 November the team rewrote the document as acceptance criteria and ran the builder again (Exhibit 3). On Friday 13 November Qasr's chief operating officer wrote that Dubai's query volumes could not be extracted at all. Figure 2 places the dates in order.

5. The people

Dilpreet Kathuria, vice-president, product, Mohali, wrote PRD v4 and pasted it in. Her bonus is written against adoption, not defects avoided, and she wants the Desk in front of hospitals before the renewal season. She has not told the committee that she ran the builder on her own initiative.

Darshil Kataria, co-founder and chief technology officer, Bengaluru, owns the 2021 rulebook decision and has defended it to three boards. He wants the prototype treated as a drawing, not as code. He has not said that two of the six material items touch rules he wrote himself and has never had reviewed.

Divjot Kamboj, engineering lead, Pune, logged nineteen divergences, more than anyone but Katoch. He is measured on sprint predictability and the Desk is two sprints late. He has not mentioned that his team had already implemented four of the thirty-one behaviours the builder chose, the same way, three weeks before the prototype existed.

Daljeet Katoch, principal claims analyst, Mohali, is one of two people who can change the rulebook and the only one at work: his colleague is on leave until Monday 30 November. He logged twenty-two divergences and five of the six material ones. He has not said that the non-payable list the builder misapplied has two versions in production, and that he knows which hospitals have which.

Devina Khattar, principal designer, Berlin, four and a half hours behind Mohali, logged fourteen divergences and one nobody else saw: the builder had invented a screen, a blocked-query state, the document never described. She wants it kept. She has not said that she proposed that screen in June and was told it was out of scope.

Dharamveer Kalia, data scientist, Toronto, ten and a half hours behind Mohali, priced the six material items and built the comparison in Exhibit 3. He has run the numbers twice and believes the second run settles the question. He has not said that he seeded the second prototype from the October extract because the September one had been archived off his laptop.

Drishika Kaundal, customer-success lead, Singapore, two and a half hours ahead, carries the support queue the Desk is meant to drain, with four people. She logged eleven divergences, three only she saw, all about what a billing clerk at four in the morning does next. She has not said that two of her largest hospitals have built their own query inbox on Sirjan's API and would rather keep it.

Davinder Kalsi, head of sales, New Jersey, ten and a half hours behind, sells the India platform to American payer-services firms and brought in Qasr. His commission on the Qasr renewal, decided on Friday 15 January 2027, is the largest line in his year. He has not said that he has already shown the prototype's screens to two prospects.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

“It never asked me a single question. Twenty-two pages, and not once ‘which do you mean’. It picked, the picks are consistent, and some are better than ours.”

Divjot Kamboj, internal chat, Wednesday 4 November, 23:10 IST

“The blocked-query screen is not a divergence. There was no screen: the document had a gap and the builder filled it. You log that as a defect because it is not in the text. I log it as the only new design work this quarter.”

Devina Khattar, email, Thursday 5 November, 14:05 Berlin, 18:35 IST

“Item B is not an ambiguity. ‘Net payable’ has one meaning in this industry: after co-payment. The sentence was wrong because nobody on the review call had ever closed a bill.”

Daljeet Katoch, triage meeting, Monday 9 November

“Nine of the thirty-one were seen by exactly one person. Three were mine, all three about night shifts. A fifth reviewer would have found more; drop any of us and the register loses one to three. Which number goes to the committee?”

Drishika Kaundal to Kathuria, Friday 13 November, 09:15 Singapore, 06:45 IST

“Thirty-one down to eleven, six material down to two, ₹371.8 lakh a month down to ₹30.9 lakh. Ninety-two per cent of the exposure, gone in eight days. Write the criteria and the problem disappears.”

Dharamveer Kalia, call notes, Friday 13 November, 07:20 Toronto, 17:50 IST

“Qasr cannot give you the Dubai numbers. Their counsel says the extract stays in the Emirates, and I am not pushing a renewal client in November. Decide without them, and do not tell them it was decided without them.”

Davinder Kalsi, email, Friday 13 November, 21:40 New Jersey, 08:10 IST Saturday 14 November

“You pasted a contract into a toy. I am not angry. I am worried that the output is now the most precise description of our product that exists, written in forty minutes by something that has never met a hospital.”

Darshil Kataria, voice note, Saturday 14 November

8. The options as Kathuria sees them

She has written four on the back of a printout; all draw on the ₹2.4 crore unspent in the FY27 product budget at 31 October.

Option 1. Adopt the prototype's behaviour as the specification. Rewrite PRD v4 to say what the prototype did on all thirty-one items, serve notice on Tuesday 17 November, pilot on the 24-hospital cohort of Exhibit 5 from Tuesday 15 December. Cost ₹58 lakh and six of the 64 engineers for four weeks. Leaves the rulebook, the Dubai deployment and the exchange conformance work untouched.

Option 2. Rewrite the document and rebuild. Four weeks writing testable acceptance criteria for all thirty-one items, a third builder run, then the verified output to the rulebook team. Cost ₹92 lakh and both claims analysts full time for the five weeks the exchange mapping needs them; notice on 11 January takes effect Monday 8 February 2027. Leaves the Dubai deployment and the 2021 rulebook architecture untouched.

Option 3. Split the module. The inbox, the ageing view and the document upload change nothing about what a hospital is told it will be paid, so they fall outside the notice clause and could go live on 1 December. All six priced items stay in the prototype. Cost ₹41 lakh, leaving ₹1.99 crore, and a second code path to hold in step. Leaves those six items, the Dubai deployment and the exchange date untouched.

Option 4. Give the builder to the hospitals. Publish the document, the sandbox and a builder template so each hospital's operations team generates its own Desk against the API, and let the divergences surface hospital by hospital. Cost ₹1.16 crore for sandbox, API hardening and support, and Kaundal's four people for the quarter. Leaves the rulebook, the notice clause, the six material items and the exchange date untouched.

Kathuria has written a fifth line on the printout and struck it out; it read “twenty-two pages, five signatures, forty minutes”.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The steering committee sits at 09:30 IST on Monday 16 November; Kathuria presents to the board on Friday 4 December. Money: ₹2.4 crore of the ₹6.0 crore FY27 product budget is unspent. People: 64 engineers, and two who can change the rulebook, one on leave until Monday 30 November. Contract: twenty working days' written notice before any change in adjudication behaviour, in every Indian agreement; Sirjan's liability is capped at ₹1.5 crore per client per year. Regulation: insurer-side conformance with the exchange is committed for the end of January 2027, and the DPDP Act governs item E whatever the resend cost says. Market: Qasr's renewal is decided on Friday 15 January 2027, its data cannot inform any of this, and Lohri on Wednesday 13 January takes the Mohali office out for two days immediately before.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What did the prototype tell Kathuria on 4 November that the 2 October review did not? Which of the six items in Exhibit 1 could a careful reader have found in PRD v4 alone?
  2. Nine of the thirty-one items in Exhibit 2 were logged by a single reviewer. What does that imply about using a divergence count as a measure of specification quality, and what would you need to know first?
  3. Exhibits 1 and 3 both price item A. Which figure would you put in front of the steering committee on Monday, and what are you assuming when you do?
  4. Kalia reads the fall from thirty-one divergences to eleven as settling the question. Exhibit 3's footnote names two things that changed besides the document, and the people section adds a third. What comparison would you have had to run instead, and what would it have cost?
  5. The notice clause was written in 2024 to reassure a hospital group. Whose interests does it protect in November 2026, and what would Sirjan give up to change it before the exchange deadline?
  6. What should Kathuria do at 09:30 on Monday 16 November, and what should she say to the board on 4 December about what this company now knows about how it writes down what it intends to build?

Mohali, Sunday night

At a quarter past eleven she took card nineteen off the wall and read it again. It said, in Katoch's hand, “working day — whose?” Below that, in her own, the word “obvious” with a line through it. The guard came up to ask whether the air conditioning should stay on. Outside, the traffic on the Chandigarh road went past the sector gate, and the thirty-one cards stayed where they were.
exp40v2-req.as.prompt:
Delivery & Technology · Requirements & Specification · Expert treatment

The spec as a prompt for an AI builder

A specification cannot be tested for clarity by the person who wrote it. A machine that never asks questions can test it — but only if you understand precisely what its silence does and does not measure.

1. Two decisions, two weeks apart

On 3 March 2026, Anand Krishnamurthy, VP Product at Vajrasetu Payments in Mumbai, had a forty-seven-requirement specification and a regulatory deadline. Vajrasetu builds recurring-payment infrastructure for lenders and subscription businesses — roughly 4.1 crore active mandates sitting on the UPI Autopay and e-mandate rails operated by NPCI under the Reserve Bank of India's framework. The feature was mandate pause and resume: letting a borrower suspend an auto-debit for one or two cycles without cancelling the mandate and re-onboarding, a flow that three of Vajrasetu's lending customers had asked for in the same quarter. The specification had been through two internal reviews. It was, in the opinion of everyone who had read it, finished.

Anand did not believe this, for a reason he could state precisely: the last three specifications he had signed off as finished had generated an average of twenty-two clarification threads during the sprint, each costing, by his engineering director's count, around 1.8 engineer-days. At Vajrasetu's fully loaded rate of about ₹24,000 an engineer-day, a "finished" spec was costing roughly ₹9.5 lakh per feature in discovered ambiguity. He had no instrument that could tell him, before the sprint, which of his forty-seven requirements would be the expensive ones.

Eleven days later and 150 kilometres away, Sharvari Deshpande, Head of Product at Virajan Learning in Pune, faced a different version of the same problem and did not recognise it as the same problem. Virajan runs a consumer test-preparation app with 2.1 million monthly active students, most of them preparing for engineering and medical entrance examinations. The feature was an adaptive revision planner: a model that looks at a student's practice history and proposes what to revise tomorrow. Her specification ran to twenty-two requirements. Nine of them described not what the software should do but how the model should behave — "prioritise topics where the student's accuracy has fallen in the last fortnight", "do not schedule more than two difficult topics on a school day", "degrade gracefully for students with fewer than thirty attempts".

Both ran their specifications through an AI builder. Anand's run produced a list that saved him most of ₹11 lakh. Sharvari's run produced a prototype that satisfied every one of her nine behavioural requirements and was, on inspection, a product she would never ship — because the builder had implemented all nine as hard-coded if-statements, which is a perfectly faithful reading of a document that never said otherwise. Her finding was not that her spec was ambiguous. It was that her spec was the wrong kind of document for the thing she was building.

The argument of this page runs from those two outcomes. The technique — handing the spec to a builder and reading what comes back as a measurement of the spec — is real, cheap and under-used. It is also a statistical instrument with a specific and calculable blind spot, and the practitioners who get burned by it are almost always the ones who did not work out what that blind spot was.

2. The idea, its history, and who disagrees about it

The definition, stated tightly: spec-as-prompt is the practice of giving an AI builder a specification as its complete instruction set, forbidding clarification, and treating the decisions the builder was forced to make as an estimate of the specification's underdetermination. The deliverable is not the software. The deliverable is a classified list of the points at which the document failed to constrain its reader.

Three terms need pinning down before anything else can be said. A specification is underdetermined at a point if two competent, good-faith readers could implement it differently there. It is ambiguous if it says something admitting two readings, and silent if it says nothing at all; both produce underdetermination and they are repaired differently. And a specification is delegating when its author knows it is silent and intends the reader to choose. Underdetermination is a property of documents. Delegation is a property of intentions. Confusing the two is the root of most of the bad practice in this area.

The lineage is long. Knuth's literate programming (1984) argued that the program and its explanation are one artefact. The executable-specification tradition — Ward Cunningham's FIT in the early 2000s, Dan North's behaviour-driven development and its Given/When/Then grammar around 2003 — made requirements runnable so that agreement could be mechanically verified rather than assumed. Formal methods went further: Z, VDM and later Alloy allowed a model checker to find contradictions no human reviewer would notice. Each of these traditions solves underdetermination by refusing it: the machine halts when the input does not determine an output.

The 2024–26 development inverts that. A large language model wired to a runtime does not halt on underdetermination; it resolves it. Given a sentence with two readings it picks one, implements it competently, and reports success. This is precisely the property that makes it useless as a verifier and valuable as an oracle: it will not tell you the spec was unclear, but it will show you, in executable form, one of the readings your document permitted. The technique is the observation that the shadow of an underdetermined document is visible in the output of a machine that must nonetheless produce something.

Four positions are genuinely held by competent practitioners, and they do not reduce to each other.

The mirror school holds that the output is worthless and the findings are everything — that the prototype should be deleted, unread by anyone outside the exercise, and that the only artefact to survive is a revised specification. It would sign: "The builder's entire value is informational; a prototype produced this way has negative option value because it anchors the team." It would not sign: "The generated code is a reasonable starting point for production."

The seed school holds the opposite: that if a builder can produce a working version of the feature in forty minutes, spending two days writing a 5,000-word document first is value destruction, and the right move is to generate, inspect, and let the running artefact become the specification. It would sign: "For anything below a certain complexity threshold, the cheapest unambiguous specification is a working prototype plus a test suite." It would not sign: "The PRD should be preserved and refined as the canonical statement of intent."

The formalist school holds that underdetermination should be removed by construction rather than detected by sampling — structured requirement grammars, typed schemas, acceptance criteria for every requirement, machine-checkable constraints — and that a non-deterministic instrument has no business inside a quality gate. It would sign: "A test whose result changes between runs cannot be a gate; at best it is exploratory." It would not sign: "Variance across builder runs is a valid measurement of specification quality."

The conversational school holds that forbidding clarifying questions is perverse: a builder that asks twelve good questions gives you the same findings in a tenth of the time, without the classification work. It would sign: "Elicitation is cheaper than divergence analysis." It would not sign: "A builder's questions are an unbiased sample of a specification's gaps." — and that refusal is the crux, because a model's questions are shaped by what it finds salient, while its silent decisions are shaped by what the document failed to say. Those are different populations.

3. Mechanics in depth, and the arithmetic nobody does

The procedural shell is uncontroversial: freeze the document, strip your own clarifications into a separate pre-run list, supply a minimal frame that is about the exercise rather than the product, require an assumptions log, read data model before state machine before error paths before copy, classify each divergence, repair, re-run. The interesting part is the statistics underneath, and here most teams are operating on an assumption that is quantitatively false.

Consider a single requirement that admits exactly two readings, X and Y. Let p be the probability that a given builder run produces reading X. Run the spec k times and diff the runs against one another. The probability that the runs are not unanimous — that the variance test detects this requirement as underdetermined — is:

Detection(k) = 1 − pk − (1 − p)k

Work the numbers. At p = 0.5, the case of a perfectly balanced ambiguity, two runs detect it with probability 1 − 0.25 − 0.25 = 0.50. Two runs catch half of the most detectable possible ambiguities. Three runs give 1 − 0.125 − 0.125 = 0.75; four runs, 0.875. The marginal return of the third run is 25 percentage points and of the fourth is 12.5, which is a steep but not worthless decline.

Now move p away from the middle, which is where real ambiguities live. Language models have strong priors; given "refund to the original payment method", most builders will do the same sensible thing most of the time. At p = 0.85 the two-run detection probability is 1 − 0.7225 − 0.0225 = 0.255. At p = 0.95 it is 0.095. At p = 0.99 it is 0.0198 — two runs will catch such a requirement about twice in a hundred attempts.

Exhibit 2. Variance-test detection probability by number of runs and prior strength, with the cumulative marginal gain of each additional run at p = 0.85.
Prior strength pk = 2k = 3k = 4k = 6
0.50 — balanced ambiguity0.5000.7500.8750.969
0.70 — mild prior0.4200.6300.7520.882
0.85 — strong prior0.2550.3830.4770.623
0.95 — very strong prior0.0950.1430.1850.265
0.99 — near-deterministic0.0200.0300.0390.059
Marginal gain at p = 0.85+0.255+0.128+0.094+0.073 / run

The second-order effect follows directly and is the single most important thing on this page. There are two distinct tests available, and they have complementary blind spots. The variance test — run against run — is objective, requires no memory of what you intended, and catches balanced ambiguities. The intent test — output against what you meant — is subjective, contaminated by hindsight, and is the only thing that catches unanimous-but-wrong readings. A team that runs only the variance test is systematically blind to the class of defect where every builder run agrees with every other and all of them disagree with the author. That class is not rare. It is produced by exactly the conditions that make a spec dangerous: domain vocabulary the model has a confident general-purpose reading of, and that your company uses to mean something else.

There is one further mechanical step that experts perform and novices do not: vocabulary isolation. Before the full run, take the glossary — every domain term the spec uses — and ask the builder to define each term operationally from the document alone, with no code. This takes four minutes and probes the dangerous quadrant directly, because it forces the model to state the prior it would otherwise apply silently. Anand added this step after his second cycle. It found three of his eleven dangerous-quadrant defects before a line of code was generated.

4. When it applies and when it does not

The conditions can be stated as testable claims rather than as advice, and it is worth applying each to both protagonists.

Claim one: the feature must be buildable in the abstract. If a faithful implementation requires systems the builder cannot see — a proprietary ledger, a partner's sandbox, a device — the output is fiction and its assumptions log describes a world that does not exist. Vajrasetu passes this only partially: pause-and-resume touches NPCI's mandate lifecycle, which the builder can only simulate. Anand's remedy was to scope the run to Vajrasetu's own orchestration layer and stub the rail, accepting that findings about rail behaviour would be worthless. Virajan passes cleanly; a revision planner needs no external system.

Claim two: the specification must be the binding constraint. The exercise measures the document, so it is useful only when the document is what the team will work from. In an organisation where engineering works from conversation and the PRD is a formality, a perfect spec changes nothing, and you have measured an artefact nobody reads.

Claim three: intent must be recoverable. The intent test requires that the author can say what they meant when shown an alternative. Where intent genuinely does not exist yet — early discovery, a feature whose shape is still being argued — there is nothing to diverge from, and the run is generative rather than diagnostic. That is legitimate but it is a different exercise with different success criteria.

Claim four: the desired behaviour must be statable as a property. This is the claim Virajan fails, and the failure is instructive. For a deterministic feature, "correct" is a property of individual outputs and prose can express it. For a model-driven feature, "correct" is a property of a distribution over outputs across a population of users, and no amount of prose specifies it. Sharvari's nine behavioural requirements were not ambiguous in the usual sense; they were category errors. The builder's unanimous decision to hard-code them was the correct reading of a document written in the wrong form.

The situation where the technique is actively misleading is worth naming plainly: a specification written in industry-standard vocabulary for a company that uses that vocabulary non-standardly. Here the builder will be confident, consistent and wrong; the variance test will return a clean bill of health; and the team will enter the sprint with more confidence than they had before, which is worse than having none.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product and platform organisations. Given a spec for one feature, a builder rebuilds every dependency it cannot see — identity, notifications, the audit log, the permission model. At Vajrasetu roughly 40 per cent of the generated code re-implemented platform services that already exist. This is not a finding about the spec and treating it as one wastes hours. The competent move is to supply a short platform context block listing what exists and must be assumed, held separate from the product spec so the exercise stays repeatable; the incompetent move is to paste the platform documentation in, which drowns the product requirements.

Two-sided and marketplace products. Every state exists at least three times — buyer, seller, operations — and builders collapse them. About half of such collapses are genuine findings and half are model artefacts, and the only reliable separator is asking, for each collapsed state, whether the spec named the other side anywhere.

Regulated products. This is where the practice needs an explicit boundary. Vajrasetu operates inside a mandate framework with prescribed notification windows and consent semantics. A constraint of that kind cannot be delegated to a stochastic reader, and builder output must never be treated as evidence of compliance — it is not an interpretation of the rules, it is a plausible-sounding guess about them. What the run can do is expose where the spec failed to state a constraint that the compliance team believed was obvious. Anand's rule, written into the team's playbook, was that every regulatory requirement carries a citation and an explicit "must not be varied" flag, and that any builder divergence on a flagged requirement is escalated rather than classified.

Hardware plus software. The builder cannot feel timing, power budgets or mechanical failure. Findings on the software side remain valid; the absence of findings about the device side means nothing at all. The characteristic error is a team reporting "no issues found in the firmware interface" when what happened is that no firmware was exercised.

AI-native products. Virajan's case generalises. When the feature's behaviour is produced by a model, the specification's centre of gravity moves from prose requirements to an evaluation set: a corpus of inputs with expected behaviour bands. Sharvari converted her nine behavioural requirements into forty eval cases — students with named histories and a stated acceptable range of planner outputs for each. That eval set, not the prose, is the thing you hand to a builder, and the divergence you read is divergence against the evals. The prose survives, but as rationale rather than as instruction.

The organisational seams. A spec usually crosses boundaries: product writes the behaviour, design owns the interaction, engineering owns the data model, support owns the failure messaging. Builder output shows you what a reader assumes when nobody has told them where the seam is. In practice the highest-value findings at both Vajrasetu and Virajan sat exactly on seams — error copy, which product assumed design owned and design assumed support owned. What mature companies say is that seam ownership is documented in a RACI; what they do is discover the seam in the sprint. The builder run moves that discovery earlier by about two weeks, and that, rather than the ambiguity count, is often where the money is.

6. Nine nuances that separate expert from competent

Unanimity is a warning, not a result. The tell is a team reporting low variance and high confidence in the same breath. An expert reads a clean variance report as a prompt to check the glossary, because the most common cause of unanimity in a domain-heavy spec is a domain word the model is confident about. The obvious reading — "the spec constrained the builder" — is right only if you have independently confirmed the constrained outcome is the one you wanted.

The assumptions log is itself a model output, and biased. Builders log the decisions they notice making. The decisions embedded in architecture — the shape of the data model, the choice of synchronous over asynchronous — frequently do not appear. The tell is a log containing twenty copy-and-validation decisions and nothing about state. The expert response is to read the schema independently of the log.

Findings are not uniformly valuable and counting them is a trap. "We found 26 ambiguities" is a vanity metric. One dangerous-quadrant defect in the refund logic is worth thirty findings about empty-state copy. Experts weight findings by the cost of discovering them late, which means the metric to track is not count but estimated avoided rework.

Repair quality is measurable and usually poor. The instinctive repair for an ambiguous requirement is to add an explanatory paragraph, which reduces variance far less than converting the requirement into a testable statement. The tell is a second-cycle variance rate that barely moves. The diagnostic is to re-run after repair — a step teams skip because the first cycle felt productive.

Specs bloat unless you delete. Every cycle adds requirements and none removes them, so documents grow monotonically until nobody reads them, at which point the whole exercise has been self-defeating. The expert habit is to run the deletion pass in the same sitting: any requirement the builder implemented identically in every run without needing it is restating a default and can go. At Vajrasetu that removed nine of forty-seven.

Delegation must be written down or it is not delegation. The tell is a PM who says "we left that to engineering" about a decision engineering did not know it owned. An explicit delegated-decisions appendix converts a silence into a commitment, and it also gives the next builder run a legitimate reason to ignore that area.

Writing for the model corrupts the document. A PRD serves engineering, design, support, sales, sometimes legal and finance. The tell is a PRD containing JSON schemas and pseudo-code. The obvious reading — "we made it precise" — is wrong: precision about implementation is not precision about intent, and the support lead can no longer read it.

Confidentiality is an engineering constraint, not a policy footnote. Real customer records, mandate identifiers and student histories do not belong in a builder run. For Indian companies the Digital Personal Data Protection Act's purpose-limitation obligations and most enterprise contracts both bite here. The expert habit is a synthetic fixture set maintained alongside the spec; the tell that a team lacks one is a prototype populated with recognisable real names.

The technique measures the document, never the idea. The most sophisticated failure in this area is a team that runs an immaculate spec-clarity process on a feature that should not exist. Clarity and validity are orthogonal, and the exercise's crispness makes it feel like progress. The tell is a team that can quote its variance rate and cannot quote its adoption hypothesis.

7. How it differs by product type and stage — and where it does not

Consumer products concentrate underdetermination in flow, state and copy; the builder produces screens cheaply, so exposure is broad and shallow. B2B and enterprise concentrate it in the permission and tenancy model, and the role hierarchy a builder invents is a precise photograph of what the spec failed to say about delegation, approval limits and audit. Platforms and marketplaces concentrate it in multi-actor state and in the boundary between what the platform guarantees and what the tenant configures. Hardware concentrates it nowhere the builder can reach, which is a statement about the instrument rather than about hardware specs. AI products relocate the specification itself, as Virajan discovered.

Stage changes purpose more than method. Early-stage teams use the run generatively: the output is richer than the spec and helps write it. Scale-ups use it diagnostically against a real codebase and must scope it tightly. Large enterprises use it politically as often as technically — a divergence found by a neutral machine settles an argument between two teams that a PM's opinion would not.

Where the difference is not real is worth saying plainly, because the literature tends to over-differentiate. The classification of divergences into silent, ambiguous, spec-wrong and model error is identical in every context. The arithmetic of Exhibit 2 does not care what you sell. And the dangerous quadrant exists everywhere, because every company has private meanings for public words.

8. Three worked examples

Exhibit 4. Three runs of the same technique, March–May 2026. Engineer-day costs are each company's fully loaded internal rate.

Vajrasetu's avoided rework: 26 intent divergences × 1.8 engineer-days × ₹24,000 = ₹11,23,200. Cost of the exercise: about ₹5,600 of model spend and 2.3 hours of the VP's time across four runs.

Vajrasetu, the clean case. Four runs surfaced nineteen run-vs-run divergences. Anand's own intent read surfaced twenty-six, of which fifteen overlapped with the variance findings, four were cases where both readings were acceptable and he chose to record them as delegated decisions, and eleven were unanimous-but-wrong. Eleven of twenty-six — 42 per cent of the real defects — were invisible to the variance test. The most expensive was requirement R-31, "the mandate resumes on the next scheduled debit date": every run resumed on the next date in the original schedule, whereas Vajrasetu's lending customers meant the next date after the pause window, which for a two-cycle pause on a monthly mandate is a different day and a different amount. Left to the sprint, that would have surfaced in integration testing, cost an estimated four engineer-days, and required a conversation with three customers.

Virajan, the reframing case. Sharvari's four runs produced only six run-vs-run divergences, all in the non-model parts of the product. Her nine behavioural requirements were implemented as fixed rules in all four runs, unanimously. Under the variance test her specification looked excellent. Under the intent test it looked like a category error, and the correct repair was not to rewrite sentences but to change the artefact: forty eval cases with named student profiles and acceptable output bands, plus a much shorter prose document explaining why those bands. Her estimate of what this avoided was six weeks — the time the team would have spent building a rules engine, demonstrating that it did not adapt, and then arguing about whether the model or the rules were at fault.

Virajmani, the failure. Virajmani Retail Systems in Hyderabad supplies replenishment software to a chain of 240 supermarkets. Its product team adopted spec-as-prompt after hearing about it, and implemented the half of it that automates: four runs, diff the runs, report the variance rate. On a thirty-four-requirement replenishment spec the variance rate came back at two of thirty-four, under 6 per cent, and the team recorded the spec as clean. It was not. The spec used the phrase "stock on hand", which at Virajmani's client means sellable units excluding damaged and customer-reserved stock, and which every builder run interpreted in its ordinary sense as total physical units. All four runs agreed. The defect sat squarely in the dangerous quadrant and the team had removed the only instrument that could see it.

The software shipped to all 240 stores. For three weeks replenishment orders were computed against inflated inventory, under-ordering fast-moving lines and over-ordering others. Virajmani's own estimate of the cost — excess and short stock, expedited deliveries, and a manual reconciliation of roughly 18,000 SKU-store pairs — was ₹41 lakh, plus a contract renegotiation. The recovery was not technical. It was three procedural changes: a glossary-definition pass before any code generation; a mandatory human intent read that cannot be delegated to the diff; and a review rule stating that a variance rate below 10 per cent on a domain-heavy spec triggers additional scrutiny rather than sign-off. The last of those is the one that matters, and it is counter-intuitive enough that it had to be written down.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

The ordering in that table is deliberate. The cheapest failures to recover from are procedural and the most expensive are epistemic. Bucket-D inflation costs you a fortnight of nobody reading the document. Variance-only testing costs you a release. Mistaking specification clarity for product validity costs you the quarter, and no amount of rigour inside the exercise protects against it, because the exercise is silent on the question by construction.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The mirror school's strongest form is an argument about anchoring. Its evidence is the observable behaviour of teams handed a working prototype: estimates drop, architecture discussion stops, and the generated data model survives into production because nobody has the energy to argue with something that already runs. On this view the prototype's option value is negative and deletion is a discipline, not a waste. For this to be wrong, teams would have to demonstrate that they can hold a running artefact and still redesign it from first principles — which some senior teams plausibly can, and most cannot.

The seed school's strongest form is an argument about cost. If a builder produces a working version of a feature in forty minutes, then a 5,000-word document written first is two days of work producing a lower-fidelity description of the same thing, and the honest reading of Vajrasetu's economics is that the document was the expensive part. Its evidence is the growing set of features that genuinely are generated rather than specified. For this to be wrong, the document would have to serve functions the artefact cannot — which it visibly does at Vajrasetu, where the PRD is read by compliance, by three customers' integration teams and by support, none of whom can read code. The disagreement therefore resolves partly by context, but not entirely: the two schools genuinely differ on whether intent can be adequately represented by a running artefact plus tests, and that is a philosophical question about representation, not an empirical one.

The formalist school's strongest form is an argument about instruments. A measurement whose result changes between runs has a variance you have not characterised, and Exhibit 2 shows that its sensitivity depends on a parameter — the model's prior strength on your particular domain language — that you cannot observe. On this view, treating a variance rate as a quality indicator is pseudo-quantification. Its evidence is Virajmani. For it to be wrong, you would have to show that a poorly characterised instrument still dominates the realistic alternative, which is no instrument at all — and that is, in fact, the mirror school's reply: the comparison is not against a formal verifier nobody will adopt, it is against a review meeting where three people say the spec looks fine.

The conversational school's strongest form is about elicitation efficiency: a builder allowed to ask questions surfaces gaps directly, in minutes, in the author's own language. Its evidence is that teams sustain question-based workflows and abandon classification-based ones. For it to be wrong, the questions would have to be a biased sample — and there is decent reason to think they are, because a model asks about what it finds salient, which correlates with what is unusual in its training distribution, not with what is underdetermined in your document. The dangerous quadrant is precisely where a model has no question to ask, because it is confident. Nobody has settled this; the honest position is that questions and silent decisions sample different parts of the defect population and a team with time should do both.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this runs the spec through a builder, produces a list, and feels productive. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four observable ways. They run the glossary pass before the build pass, because they know the dangerous quadrant is made of vocabulary. They never let the variance diff substitute for a human reading the output against intent, and they treat a low variance rate on a domain-heavy document as a reason for more scrutiny rather than less. They delete requirements in the same sitting in which they add them, so the document stays readable by the five constituencies that depend on it. And they hold the boundary of the instrument without being asked: when a colleague says the builder run shows the feature is sound, they say that it shows the document is clear, which is a smaller and more useful claim.

The deeper marker is that they have a view on how many runs to do and can defend it with the arithmetic. Four runs at p = 0.85 gets you 48 per cent detection; six gets 62 per cent; the marginal run beyond that costs more attention than it returns, and attention spent instead on a careful intent read of the schema buys far more. Mastery here looks less like enthusiasm for the technique and more like a calibrated sense of what fraction of the defects it will never find.

12. What they decided

Anand kept the exercise and constrained it. Vajrasetu's playbook now requires a glossary pass, four runs, both tests, a delegated-decisions appendix and a deletion pass, and forbids builder output from appearing in any compliance artefact. The revised spec went into the sprint at forty-two requirements, five fewer than it started with. His stated reasoning was that the technique had bought him a forty-two per cent improvement in pre-sprint defect detection and that he now knew, numerically, the size of the part it could not see — and that the second of those was the more valuable purchase.

Sharvari changed the artefact rather than the process. Virajan's specifications for model-driven features are now eval sets with prose rationale attached, and the builder run is executed against the evals. She did not conclude that spec-as-prompt had failed her; she concluded that it had correctly diagnosed a document written in the wrong form, which is the most useful finding the technique can produce and the one that is hardest to hear.

Three questions in the manner of a teaching note. First: Virajmani's team implemented the automatable half of the technique and skipped the half requiring judgement, which is what organisations reliably do — what would you change about how the practice is taught so that the judgement half is the part that survives contact with a busy team? Second: the seed school's cost argument applies with full force to Virajan's consumer feature and barely at all to Vajrasetu's regulated one; is that a difference of domain, of company stage, or of who the document's readers are — and which of those would you expect to change in three years? Third: if you accept that the variance test is blind to unanimous-but-wrong readings, and that those readings are produced by private meanings of public words, what does that imply about which parts of a specification deserve the most editorial effort?

13. Going deeper

PRD structure is the prerequisite that makes the exercise legible: a document with numbered, individually addressable requirements can be scored requirement by requirement, and an essay cannot. It unlocks the ability to report variance as a rate rather than an impression.

Prompting a builder from a spec covers the frame — stack, run instructions, the prohibition on questions, the assumptions log — and matters next because a badly framed run produces findings about the frame rather than about the document.

What a PRD becomes when the reader can build takes the argument one step further: if the document's first reader acts on it immediately, the economics of writing it change, and so does what belongs in it and what should be deleted.

PM artefacts: one-pager, PRD, spec, strategy doc matters because the Virajan finding was fundamentally an artefact-selection error, and knowing the repertoire is what lets you recognise one.

Writing a one-pager is the discipline of stating intent before detail, which is what protects the deletion pass: you cannot tell which requirements are restating defaults unless you know what the feature is for.

Customer narratives (Day 0 / Day N) supply the intent against which output is read — the intent test needs a written statement of the intended experience or it degrades into the author's memory.

Acceptance criteria and error cases is the single highest-leverage follow-on: a requirement in Given/When/Then form has far fewer honest readings, and error cases are where builders default hardest to the happy path.

Telemetry requirements matter because builders almost never invent instrumentation and their silence there is uninformative — you have to specify it, and the run will not remind you.

Non-functional requirements closes the instrument's largest structural blind spot: latency, idempotency, tenancy isolation, data handling and audit are systematically under-exercised by a prototype, so an absence of findings in those areas means nothing.

The spec as a prompt for an AI builder

Hand the PRD to the builder, and read what comes back not as software but as a confession: every place the machine had to decide something is a place you failed to.

1. Bengaluru, February 2026

On the evening of 9 February 2026, Meghna Iyer, Director of Product at Vajrika Commerce Cloud, had a nine-page document open on one screen and a sprint plan on the other, and she did not believe either of them.

Vajrika sells storefront and order-management software to mid-market direct-to-consumer brands in India — thirty-eight customers, most of them apparel and home-goods labels doing between ₹4 crore and ₹90 crore a year. The feature under discussion was partial returns with instant refund: a shopper who bought three items keeps two, returns one, and is refunded for that one item before the courier has physically brought it back. Roughly ₹1.2 crore of merchandise value passes through Vajrika's returns pipeline on an ordinary weekday, and about a fifth of it is partial. Two of Vajrika's largest customers had said, in writing, that they would not renew without it.

Meghna's PRD ran to 2,800 words and thirty-one numbered requirements. Her engineering lead, Farhan Qureshi, had read it twice and come back with a sprint estimate of nineteen days against a fourteen-day sprint, and a request to cut the refund-reversal logic. Meghna suspected the estimate was not really about scope. It was about the eleven questions Farhan had not yet asked her, which would arrive one at a time on Slack over the following fortnight, each one stalling a developer for half a day. She had been through this on the last two features. The spec had felt complete when she wrote it and had turned out to contain, in the engineers' phrase, "a lot of weather."

What she did that evening was unusual only in that she did it deliberately. She pasted the PRD, unedited, into an AI coding agent, told it to build a working prototype, forbade it from asking her any clarifying questions, and required it to keep a log of every decision it had to make on its own. She was not trying to get software. She was trying to get a list.

2. The idea, stated precisely

The technique goes by several names — spec-as-prompt, builder-as-reviewer, ambiguity harvesting — and the definition that matters is this: you give an AI builder your specification as the whole of its instructions, and you treat the gap between what it produced and what you intended as a measurement of how ambiguous your specification is. The artefact of interest is not the code. It is the set of decisions the builder made that you did not make for it.

An AI builder, for our purposes, is a large language model wired to a file system and a runtime, capable of writing and executing code across many files — the category that includes agentic coding tools and prototype generators. A specification or PRD is the document that states what is to be built and why. An ambiguity is a sentence in that document admitting more than one faithful reading; an omission is a question the document does not address at all. Both produce the same symptom downstream, which is why practitioners tend to lump them together, and why it is worth keeping them apart.

The problem this technique was invented to solve is old and specific: a written specification cannot be tested for clarity by its author, because the author reads it with the intent already in their head. Every word of a PRD is unambiguous to the person who wrote it. The intellectual lineage runs through Donald Knuth's literate programming in 1984, which argued that programs should be written to be read; through the executable-specification tradition of the early 2000s, when Dan North and colleagues formalised behaviour-driven development and its Given / When / Then grammar precisely so that a requirement could be run rather than merely agreed; and through formal methods, where specification languages such as Z and Alloy let a model checker find contradictions a human reader would slide past.

What changed around 2024 is not the ambition but the mechanism, and the difference is worth sitting with because it is the crux of the whole technique. A compiler, a type checker and a model checker all halt on ambiguity. They stop and tell you the specification is underdetermined. A language model does the opposite: it resolves ambiguity, silently, plausibly, and with complete confidence, because resolving underdetermined input into fluent output is the thing it was built to do. That property is a defect if you want a compiler and a gift if you want a mirror. The builder will never tell you your spec was unclear. It will simply show you, in working code, one of the readings your spec permitted — and if that reading is not the one you meant, you have found a hole.

The sentence Meghna could say in a meeting, without sounding like she was quoting a newsletter, was this: "I ran the spec through a builder. It didn't ask me anything, which is the point — it made twenty-three decisions instead, and eleven of them were wrong. Those eleven are the questions Farhan would have asked me over the next two weeks."

3. How it actually works

The mechanics are simple to describe and surprisingly easy to get wrong, mostly because the instinct to produce a good prototype fights the goal of producing a good diagnosis. There are seven steps, and the third and sixth are the ones practitioners leave implicit.

Freeze the spec. Use the document exactly as it stands, the version you would have handed to engineering. The temptation to tidy it first is the temptation to destroy the measurement.

Strip your own scaffolding. Whatever you feel compelled to add to the prompt — "note that refunds go to store credit if the card is expired", "the brand admin is a different role from the ops user" — do not add it. Write it on a separate list instead. That list is your first finding, produced before the builder has run a single line. Meghna's pre-run list had four items on it, all four of which turned out to be genuine spec omissions.

Frame, do not explain. The builder needs a minimum frame that is not part of the product spec: the stack to use, how to run it, that it must not ask clarifying questions, and that it must produce an assumptions log — a file listing every decision it made that the spec did not determine. The frame is about the exercise; the spec is about the product. Keeping them separate is what makes the run repeatable.

Read in a fixed order. Data model first, then state transitions, then error and failure paths, then user-visible copy, then the assumptions log. This order runs from the least reversible to the most reversible decision. Reading the screens first — the natural instinct — anchors you on aesthetics and you will never get to the state machine.

Classify every divergence. Each place the builder's output differs from your intent falls into one of four buckets, and the classification is the whole intellectual content of the exercise.

Measure variance, not just divergence. This is the step most teams skip and the one that makes the method trustworthy. Run the identical spec twice — two sessions, or two different builders — and diff the two outputs against each other rather than against your intent. Where the two runs agree, the spec constrained them; where they disagree, the spec left the decision open. Variance between runs is a cleaner ambiguity signal than divergence from intent, because it does not depend on your memory of what you meant. It also separates bucket B from bucket D almost automatically: a genuine ambiguity produces two different plausible readings, while a model error produces one thing that is simply wrong in both runs, or wrong in ways unrelated to the text.

Repair, then re-run. Rewrite the spec and run again. If the variance does not fall, your repair did not repair anything — which happens more often than people expect, because the natural fix is to add a paragraph of explanation rather than a testable statement.

4. The worked example, line by line

Meghna's PRD contained thirty-one numbered requirements. She ran it twice on the night of 9 February, in two clean sessions, and spent the morning of the tenth diffing the outputs. The arithmetic is worth following precisely.

Exhibit 3. Vajrika Commerce Cloud — PRD "Partial returns with instant refund", two-run diagnostic, 9–10 February 2026. Thirty-one numbered requirements.
MeasureRun ARun BA vs B
Requirements implemented at all2931—
Entries in assumptions log2326—
Requirements implemented differently in A and B——11
Two-run variance rate——35.5%
Classified A (silent) / B (ambiguous) / C (spec wrong)9 / 7 / 211 / 8 / 218 unique
Classified D (model error, discarded)55—

Read the third row first. Eleven of thirty-one requirements — 11 ÷ 31 = 35.5 per cent — were implemented one way by run A and a different way by run B. Requirement R-14, quoted in Exhibit 1, is a fair sample: run A refunded to the original card and failed silently when the card token had expired; run B detected the expired token and issued store credit, inventing a store-credit ledger that Vajrika does not have. Neither behaviour is wrong given the sentence. The sentence is wrong.

The twenty-three and twenty-six log entries overlapped heavily; de-duplicated, there were eighteen distinct spec defects across the two runs plus five model errors that appeared in both. Meghna rewrote eleven requirements, added four that had not existed, deleted three that turned out to be restating platform defaults, and added a one-page appendix headed Decisions delegated to engineering listing six choices she was explicitly not making.

The second pass: change one input. On the afternoon of the tenth she ran the revised spec twice more. The only input that changed was the document; the frame, the stack instruction and the model were identical. Variance fell from eleven requirements to three — 3 ÷ 31 = 9.7 per cent. Two of the remaining three were the delegated decisions, which she was content to leave open. One was a genuine residual ambiguity in the reversal window, which she fixed by hand in ninety seconds.

The economics are the part that persuaded Farhan. Vajrika's fully loaded engineering day costs roughly ₹19,000. Historical data from the previous two features suggested that a spec ambiguity discovered mid-sprint cost on average 1.4 engineer-days — the interrupted developer, the clarification thread, the rework, the re-review. Eight closed ambiguities × 1.4 × ₹19,000 comes to ₹2.13 lakh of avoided rework, against roughly four hours of Meghna's time and about ₹1,100 of model spend. Even discounting heavily for the ambiguities Farhan would have absorbed without telling anyone, the ratio is not close.

The prototype was worth nothing. The eighteen-line list of things it had to decide for itself was worth about thirteen engineer-days.

5. Eight nuances you have to hold

Silence is not agreement. The single most common error is to read a clean-looking prototype as evidence of a clean spec. The builder does not ask questions; that is a property of the tool, not a verdict on the document. If you did not demand an assumptions log, you did not run the experiment — you just generated some code.

Omission, ambiguity and delegation are three different things. A gap in the spec may be a defect, or it may be a deliberate handover: "the team picks the retry backoff" is a legitimate position. The failure is not having the gap; it is not knowing whether the gap is intentional. A good spec makes its delegations explicit, and the builder run is the cheapest way to find out which of your silences you actually meant.

Model error must be separated from spec defect, and the separator is repetition. A single run cannot tell you whether the builder misread you or you misled it. Two runs usually can. Treating every strange output as a specification failure is how a nine-page PRD becomes a thirty-page PRD full of defensive clauses that no human being will ever read.

Fluency is the enemy of inspection. A prototype that looks finished — styled, animated, populated with convincing data — stops people from looking underneath it. Some teams deliberately ask the builder for unstyled output for this reason. The polish is real and the correctness is not, and the two arrive together.

"It works" and "it is right" are unrelated claims. The test here is fidelity to intent, not functionality. A prototype can pass every test the builder wrote for itself and still implement a product nobody asked for, because the builder wrote the tests from the same ambiguous sentences.

The method is silent on whether the thing is worth building. This is an internal consistency check, not a market test. It will tell you that R-14 is ambiguous. It will not tell you that partial returns are the wrong bet, that brands will not adopt them, that the unit economics of instant refund are negative at Vajrika's RTO rate, or that the architecture will collapse at ten times the volume. Confusing a clarity test for a validity test is the fastest way to build a beautifully specified mistake.

Non-functional requirements are systematically under-exposed. Builders default to the happy path. Latency budgets, idempotency under retries, tenant isolation, personal-data handling, audit trails and rate limits are rarely exercised by a prototype at all, so the absence of findings in those areas is meaningless. You have to probe them deliberately, by asking the builder to write the failure cases rather than the feature. For an Indian SaaS company the personal-data question is not abstract: obligations under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act and customers' own contractual terms mean the run should use synthetic records, never a slice of production.

Do not write the PRD for the builder. A PRD has several audiences — engineering, design, support, sales, sometimes legal and finance. Over-fitting it to what a model parses well, with schema dumps and pseudo-code, degrades it for every human reader. The correct response to a builder run is a clearer document, which is usually a shorter one, not a machine-readable one.

6. How it differs by product type and company stage

The technique is the same everywhere; what it finds is not. In consumer products the ambiguity concentrates in flow and copy — empty states, interrupted journeys, what the screen says when the payment is pending. The builder generates screens quickly and cheaply, so the exposure is broad and shallow, and the most valuable findings tend to be states nobody had named.

In B2B and enterprise software the ambiguity concentrates in the permission model. Given a spec that says "the admin can approve refunds", a builder will invent an entire role hierarchy, and the role hierarchy it invents is an exact photograph of what your spec failed to say about tenancy, delegation, approval limits and audit. Vajrika is a B2B company and eight of its eighteen findings were of this kind.

Marketplaces have the hardest version of the problem, because every state exists three times: what the buyer sees, what the seller sees, and what operations sees. Builders reliably collapse the two sides into one, which is a genuine finding roughly half the time — the spec really did describe only one side — and a model artefact the other half.

Stage changes the purpose more than the method. At an early-stage company the builder's output is often richer than the spec, and the run is generative: you use it to discover what the spec should contain. At a company of Vajrika's size, with an existing schema, a design system and a support organisation, most of the output is irrelevant by construction, and the run is diagnostic: you scope it tightly to the new surface and read only the assumptions log. Running an unscoped builder against a mature codebase produces a great deal of confident output about a system that does not exist.

7. Four mistakes, and the cheapest diagnostic for each

Shipping the prototype. The symptom is visible from outside: a demo to a customer or a board within days of the run, or a Slack message proposing that the team "start from what the builder made". The underlying misunderstanding is treating the artefact as the output when the list was the output. The diagnostic costs one question — "which of the thirty-one requirements has a test that a human wrote?" — and the answer is almost always none.

Prompting around the gaps. The symptom is a prompt three times the length of the PRD, thick with clarifications. The misunderstanding is optimising for good output instead of honest input. The diagnostic is mechanical: diff the prompt against the document, and treat every clause present in one and absent from the other as a finding rather than a fix.

Treating every divergence as your fault. The symptom is spec bloat — the document doubles, and the new material is defensive detail about things no engineer would have asked. The diagnostic is a single question per item: "would a competent engineer on my team have asked me this?" If not, it belongs in bucket D.

Running it once. The symptom is a confident readout with no uncertainty in it. The misunderstanding is thinking of the builder as a deterministic instrument. The diagnostic is simply to run it again and see how much of the readout survives; at Vajrika, five of twenty-three log entries did not.

8. What good looks like

By April, Vajrika's version of this had become a forty-minute ritual that happened the day before spec review, not the day after. Meghna froze the document, ran it twice with an assumptions log required and styling suppressed, diffed the runs against each other before diffing either against her intent, classified every entry into the four buckets in front of Farhan rather than alone, and brought two artefacts to the review: a revised spec, and a one-page appendix of decisions deliberately delegated. The revised specs were, on average, slightly shorter than the originals, because the exercise deleted as many requirements as it added. Sprint-time clarification threads on the two features that followed fell from an average of eleven to three.

9. What Meghna decided

She did not ship the prototype; she deleted both copies on 10 February, partly on principle and partly because they contained an invented store-credit ledger that she did not want anyone to see and mistake for a plan. She rewrote eleven requirements, added four, deleted three, and published the delegated-decisions appendix. Farhan's estimate came back at thirteen days against the fourteen-day sprint, and the refund-reversal logic stayed in scope — not because the work got smaller, but because the uncertainty did.

Her reasoning, recorded in the sprint notes, was narrow and defensible: the builder had told her nothing about whether partial returns were a good idea, and everything about whether her document described one. Those are different questions and she had only bought an answer to the second.

What to learn next follows directly. Acceptance criteria and error cases is the discipline that closes bucket B permanently, because a requirement written as Given / When / Then has far fewer honest readings than a requirement written as a sentence. Non-functional requirements addresses the blind spot the method cannot see on its own. And What a PRD becomes when the reader can build takes the argument one step further: if the document's first reader is a machine that will act on it immediately, the economics of writing it change, and so does what belongs in it.

Two questions to sit with. First: if your specification produced no divergences at all on two independent runs, would that be evidence that it is excellent, or evidence that it is so detailed that it has stopped being a specification and become an implementation? Second: of the silences in your current spec, how many could you defend in front of your engineering lead as deliberate delegations — and what does your answer tell you about the ones you could not?
